messages.content:
A learner of Spanish (own language English) just revised a piece for Email to a Spanish language school. These are the parts that changed:
1. They first wrote: "Vengo por mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy excitado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   It ended as: "Vengo a mejorar mi español por mi novia, que es de Granada. El año pasado conocí a su familia, pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   What was wrong: The main reason is hard to find, because the opening sentence runs the girlfriend, the family meeting, the failure to understand and the eagerness to learn into one long run without a clear purpose.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: por mi novia, que es de Granada: Ties the reason to the purpose in one clause, instead of a colon that leaves the reader to work out the link. Without it, the sentence reads as a list of facts. / El año pasado conocí a su familia, pero: Splitting here gives the meeting its own sentence, so the 'pero' contrast lands clearly. Chaining everything with 'y' or ':' blurs the failure into the rest.
2. They first wrote: "¿Es posible que usted me envía información sobre los precios?"
   It ended as: "¿Le agradecería que me enviara información sobre los precios?"
   What was wrong: The request is framed as whether it is possible, which invites a literal yes or no rather than asking directly, usually with podría.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
3. They first wrote: "(I'm not picky but I don't eat meat)"
   It ended as: "(en lo demás soy muy flexible, pero no como carne)"
   What was wrong: The English parenthetical is left in English and the Spanish reader cannot read it. The key point, that Daniel is flexible about everything except meat, is missing.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
4. They first wrote: "Mirando adelante a oír de usted."
   It ended as: "Quedo a la espera de su respuesta."
   What was wrong: This is a direct translation of the English closing Looking forward to hearing from you. Spanish readers expect a closing like Espero su respuesta, so this sounds foreign at the end of a formal letter.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: Quedo a la espera de: This is the fixed formal way Spanish letters express 'looking forward to'. Writing 'Mirando adelante' or 'Espero' alone either calques English or drops the sense of anticipation that 'looking forward' carries. / respuesta: Spanish readers expect the noun for the reply. 'Oír de usted' is a literal translation of 'hear from you' and sounds foreign at the close of a formal letter. / su: Keep the formal possessive to match the usted address used throughout the letter; 'tu' would break the register.
5. They first wrote: "espero que la familia pueda cocinar algo para mí"
   It ended as: "pero no como carne). ¿Sería posible que la familia cocinara algo para mí sin carne?"
   What was wrong: Espero que followed by the family cooking presents the family's cooking as an expected duty. The reader, who manages the housing, may feel pressured rather than asked.
   How: they rebuilt this part with the tutor
   The tutor's notes on the new wording: cocinara: After 'sería posible que' the verb takes the imperfect subjunctive, so 'pueda' becomes 'cocinara'. The past form also makes the request sound more tentative, like 'pueda' in the draft did not. / sin carne: 'Sin carne' names the exact thing he needs. The draft's 'algo para mí' leaves the family guessing what kind of food, and this dish could easily include meat.
6. They first wrote: "Vengo por mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy excitado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   It ended as: "Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."
   What was wrong: estoy muy excitado → tengo muchas ganas: 'Estar excitado' in Spanish usually means sexually aroused, so it would embarrass the reader. 'Tener ganas de' expresses eagerness to learn.
   How: the tutor corrected it
7. They first wrote: "¿Es el piso cerca de la escuela?"
   It ended as: "¿Está el piso cerca de la escuela?"
   What was wrong: ¿Es → ¿Está: A location is expressed with 'estar', not 'ser', so 'Está el piso cerca...' is the correct form.
   How: the tutor corrected it
8. They first wrote: "¿Me puedes decir cuándo empiezan los cursos?"
   It ended as: "¿Me puede decir cuándo empiezan los cursos?"
   What was wrong: puedes → puede: The letter uses formal 'usted' with Sra. Morales, so this question should use the third person 'puede' rather than the informal 'puedes'.
   How: the tutor corrected it
9. They first wrote: "Estoy seguro de que voy a tener un buen tiempo en su escuela."
   It ended as: "Estoy seguro de que voy a pasar muy bien en su escuela."
   What was wrong: tener un buen tiempo → pasar muy bien: 'Tener un buen tiempo' is a direct translation of 'have a good time' and is not how Spanish speakers say it. 'Pasarlo muy bien' is the standard expression.
   How: the tutor corrected it

Their notebook keeps Spanish expressions to review later. For each part, first lesson: what the change teaches, in a few English words. Then file: whether it earns an entry. An entry is worth filing only when the change teaches a reusable Spanish expression this writer did not have: a word in the sense meant here, which verb, preposition or adjective goes with which word, a set phrase or formula, the way this community says something. Not worth filing: a grammar rule applied (agreement, tense, mood, articles, gender, word order, a missing verb), spelling, accents, punctuation and capitals, a fact or a name put right, one of the writer's own alternatives picked, and words a writer at their level already uses (judge their level from what the draft already gets right).
One entry per expression: when two parts teach the same one, file it with the first and not again.
For a part you file, write the entry:
- phrase: the expression the change taught, copied from how it ended (words that are not in it never go in): the words that do the job the change was about, not the sentence's frame around them; as a learner would file it ("topped with", "it's not anyone's fault"), at most six words, "…" only where a slot really varies; no letters such as X or Y, no translation, no grammar terms.
- meaning: in English, one short line: what it means or does, in the sense it has here.
- usage: in English, one or two short sentences: when people use it and what it goes with (register when it matters), and what makes it better than what they first wrote when that is the point.
- examples: three short, natural Spanish sentences using it in exactly the sense it has here (if it has other senses, as "our own" means both "made by us" and "belonging to us", never those), each with its English translation (n): one in a situation like theirs (not their own sentence again), two in everyday situations far from it, built differently around it so they see how it is used, not one frame. Names of people, characters, places and groups stay exactly as the piece writes them, in the translations too (never a translated or transliterated name).
For a part you do not file, give only n, lesson and file.
The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in English.
Reply with JSON only: {"notes":[{"n":1,"lesson":"","file":true,"phrase":"","meaning":"","usage":"","examples":[{"t":"","n":""}]},{"n":2,"lesson":"","file":false}]}

It is followed by the subjunctive, and it is more direct and courteous than asking whether something is possible.","examples":[{"t":"Le agradecería que me confirmara la fecha de inicio.","n":"I would be grateful if you could confirm the start date for me."},{"t":"Le agradecería que cerrara la puerta al salir.","n":"I would appreciate it if you would close the door when you leave."},{"t":"Le agradecería que me devolviera el paraguas mañana.","n":"I would be grateful if you could give me back the umbrella tomorrow."}]},{"n":3,"lesson":"Rendering 'otherwise' or 'apart from that' with a fixed phrase rather than translating word for word.","file":true,"phrase":"en lo demás","meaning":"as for everything else; otherwise","usage":"Used to set one exception or problem apart from the rest of a statement, usually after a 'pero' clause. It is natural in everyday speech and in polite written requests.","examples":[{"t":"Quiero una habitación tranquila; en lo demás me adapto sin problema.","n":"I want a quiet room; as for everything else, I adapt without any problem."},{"t":"El restaurante era caro, pero en lo demás el servicio fue excelente.","n":"The restaurant was expensive, but otherwise the service was excellent."},{"t":"En lo demás, todo salió bien.","n":"Apart from that, everything went well."}]},{"n":4,"lesson":"Closing a formal letter with the fixed expression for looking forward, not a calque.","file":true,"phrase":"Quedo a la espera de","meaning":"I look forward to / I await","usage":"The standard formal way to close a letter or email, followed by a noun for the reply. Avoid calquing 'looking forward to' or using a bare 'espero' at the end of formal letters.","examples":[{"t":"Quedo a la espera de su confirmación.","n":"I look forward to your confirmation."},{"t":"Quedo a la espera de noticias del banco.","n":"I am waiting to hear from the bank."},{"t":"Quedo a la espera de los resultados de la prueba.","n":"I look forward to the results of the test."}]},{"n":5,"lesson":"Tentative request via subjunctive grammar and naming the exact need; the rule applied is grammar.","file":false},{"n":6,"lesson":"Expressing eagerness with a set verb phrase instead of the false friend 'excitado'.","file":true,"phrase":"tener ganas de","meaning":"to feel like; to be keen to","usage":"The everyday way to express wanting or eagerness to do something. Use it instead of 'estar excitado', which in Spanish suggests sexual arousal.","examples":[{"t":"Tengo muchas ganas de hablar con tu familia.","n":"I'm really keen to talk with your family."},{"t":"Después del examen, tenía ganas de dormir.","n":"After the exam, I just felt like sleeping."},{"t":"¿Tienes ganas de un café?","n":"Do you fancy a coffee?"}]},{"n":7,"lesson":"Location is expressed with estar, a grammar rule applied.","file":false},{"n":8,"lesson":"Formal usted requires the third-person verb form, a grammar rule applied.","file":false},{"n":9,"lesson":"Saying 'have a good time' with the fixed expression 'pasarlo muy bien' instead of translating literally.","file":true,"phrase":"pasarlo muy bien","meaning":"to have a really good time","usage":"The standard way to say you enjoy yourself or will have a good time, in both casual and polite speech. Literal translations like 'tener un buen tiempo' sound foreign.","examples":[{"t":"Seguro que lo vamos a pasar muy bien en la clase.","n":"We'll surely have a really good time in the class."},{"t":"Los niños lo pasaron muy bien en la playa.","n":"The children had a really good time at the beach."},{"t":"¿Lo pasaste muy bien en la fiesta?","n":"Did you have a really good time at the party?"}]}]}
